```{python}
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from IPython.display import Markdown

R = Path("../results/router")
pol = pd.read_csv(R / "policies.csv")
u = pd.read_parquet(R / "units.parquet")
```

::: {.callout-note title="Intuition"}
A router is a bet: for some series the shared zero-shot model is good enough, or better, and a dedicated model
is a waste. For others, the dedicated model is worth its upkeep. The router is right if (a) such series exist and
(b) it can recognise them **before** seeing the test period.
:::

## Do such series exist?

![](figures/router_units.png)

```{python}
g = u.groupby("history")[["loss_spec", "loss_tsfm", "cov90_spec", "cov90_tsfm"]].mean()
g.index = ["1 week", "2 weeks", "4 weeks", "12 weeks"]
g.columns = ["specialist MASE", "TSFM MASE", "specialist cov90", "TSFM cov90"]
Markdown(g.round(3).to_markdown())
```

On load, no. Chronos-2 wins on **all 200 units**, by 5% to 70%. The gap is widest in cold start, where the
specialist cannot see two weekly cycles and its intervals under-cover badly.

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out: this is load against univariate specialists"}
The paper's specialists are supervised models, and its "physical" regime is transformer oil temperature. A
load specialist in production would have temperature and holiday inputs. This panel says nothing against such a
specialist. It says that a univariate one refitted daily is beaten everywhere.
:::

## The pre-registered policies

```{python}
t = pol[pol.history == "all"].set_index("policy")[["mase", "cov90", "share_tsfm", "diff_vs_tsfm", "diff_lo", "diff_hi"]]
Markdown(t.round(3).to_markdown())
```

The paper's thresholds, applied as published, keep 8% of series on the specialist and lose 0.030 MASE. The
stump learned leave-one-country-out never finds a better split than "always TSFM".

## What a cost-aware router buys

![](figures/router_frontier.png)

::: {.callout-important title="An oracle is not a policy"}
The red curve sorts units by their **realised** gain: it is the best any router could do, and it needs the answer.
The paper's headline (0.970, a 70% cost cut) is such a curve. Out of sample, our stump stays within 0.015 MASE of
it between 25% and 100% of TSFM calls. The paper's rule sits above the random line.
:::

And the cost itself: Chronos-2 takes about 95 ms per series on 4 CPU threads, or about 5 ms in a GPU batch.
An MSTL refit takes 183 ms on one core. The paper's assumed 1000x ratio describes a specialist that only
predicts. A specialist that refits every day costs as much as the TSFM.

## The router drifts

![](figures/router_drift.png)

::: {.callout-tip title="Takeaway"}
Re-evaluated every 5 days on the trailing 4 weeks, a cost-aware rule on acf_24 moves 40 of 50 series and
swings the TSFM share from 12% to 78%. A ±0.05 hysteresis band cuts the flips from 323 to 78. A router is a
model: it needs its own monitoring, its own owner and versioned thresholds.
:::
